title: Home Invasion!
author: Ewan Shepherd
source: FFT Tutoring with the Lightning Squad (tutoring.fft.org.uk), screenshots supplied 6 Oct 2026

pages.heading: A Long Summer
pages.text: It had been a long summer. I had been away for most of it, stuck on a family trip, catching up with my cousins. I never really liked holidays like that – where you buddy up with your uncle’s family, or your parents’ friends. I never had anything in common with the other kids – they loved wrestling and card games, but I didn’t. I liked drawing, reading comic books, and watching the football – but definitely not playing it. I wasn’t a very competitive person.
pages.imageAlt: A pixel-art boy looking bored on a holiday sofa, surrounded by his cousins and relatives.

pages.heading: Go and Play Outside
pages.text: I always hated how on those big holidays - when there were loads of us – the grown-ups would say “Why don’t you kids go and play outside?” My older brother said they just wanted to get rid of us. He stopped going on those trips a while ago. Whenever they said it, what always ended up happening was this: I sat on a bench while my two cousins wrestled each other. I recoiled when they’d tell me to get involved. It was usually then that I texted my friends.

pages.heading: Texting Friends
pages.text: Joe was in Spain for the summer holidays. The pool didn’t have any water in it, so his parents complained at the front desk. EVERY. DAY. Katie’s dad had taken her to Brussels for her birthday. They stayed with his cousin. I always found it weird to think that grown-ups have cousins. Then, I would text Alex. His parents had busy jobs – they’d spent the summer travelling around and working late. He had been home alone most of the holidays. Alex never responded to my texts.

pages.heading: Still No Word
pages.text: When I finally returned from my holidays, school was back on the horizon. All the supermarkets had the new lunchboxes and stationary out. I only had a limited amount of time to reclaim the fun I was promised on the last day before the break. Then, I thought about Alex. Before I could focus on having the best end-of-summer ever, I had to check on him. I had to make sure everything was OK. I checked my phone again. Still no word from him.
pages.imageAlt: A pixel-art hand holding a phone with a question mark and 'Alex?' on the screen.

pages.heading: A Strange Sound
pages.text: I wasn’t worried. Alex didn’t really use his phone and didn’t have any big apps or anything. In fact, until his last birthday, he just used his mum’s phone whenever we went out. I’d known him since we were six, and I’d only seen him lose his temper once. He just kept his head down, always stayed friendly and didn’t talk much. That’s why it was important I made the effort - as his friend - to make sure that he was OK. There was no chance he would ever just tell me. The weather was warm, so I decided to walk to his house. When I got to his door and went to ring the bell, I heard a strange whirring sound.

pages.heading: The Web Camera
pages.text: I looked up and saw it was coming from an old web camera – that kind that you used to plug into your computer or laptop before they came with their own. We had one at home. It had sat in a drawer in my kitchen for… my entire life. It was bolted into the top of Alex’s doorframe. I stared up at it. It stared right back. Then, the lock clicked! The door popped open, and I heard his voice from up the stairs. “Hi Jack!” It was Alex. “Hello!” I shouted up.
pages.imageAlt: A pixel-art security camera above a front door, with a boy standing at the door.

pages.heading: The Coat Stand
pages.text: Dusty air was floating in the light that had broken through the open door. I peeked down the corridor when suddenly the coat stand leant forward to take my hoodie! It was attached to an old weighing scale, which had been modified with some electronic hinges. Did Alex make those himself? “I’m in my room!” he yelled. I slowly extended my arm to give the stand my jacket and it leant back into position. I kept looking back as I cautiously made my way up the stairs. I couldn’t believe what I was seeing! The front door slowly closed itself. The lock clicked into position and the latch whirred shut. How had Alex done all of this in just a few weeks?

pages.heading: Alex’s Room
pages.text: When I got to his bedroom, I saw Alex sitting at his computer. It was very… retro. A proper grey box - like one from an old movie. The monitor sounded out of breath. I could hear it humming – it sounded like overheating. How long until it started steaming? He would be heartbroken when that grey box finally broke down. Then again, Alex could probably fix it. He was an electronics whizz – he could engineer the coolest stuff! I went round to his house a few years ago and he had made an operational light with old circuit-boards and wires. It had four different colours: red, blue, yellow, and green. As I looked around his room, and saw his computer desk - littered with wires and pliers, screwdrivers and batteries - I couldn’t help but get the feeling that this summer, Alex had come a long way from lights that had four different colours… His phone was stuck between his bed and the wall. I could just see it disappearing. Clearly, he had been focussed on other things.
pages.imageAlt: A pixel-art boy at an old computer in a bedroom crammed with wires and gadgets.

pages.heading: Watch This
pages.text: “Did you do all that stuff with the door? The coat stand?” I asked. “I did a lot more than just that,” he replied. “Watch this.” Alex typed a combination of keys into his computer. The screen was an eerie black with pixelated writing on it that came up in all sorts of weird colours. It looked like an old arcade game. “Let’s head downstairs,” he said with a grin. He sounded so confident, so proud. The walls around us suddenly started to hum and the floor started to vibrate. There was an energy surrounding us that hadn’t been there when I entered the house a few minutes ago. It was as if Alex had brought it to life.

pages.heading: Dance Partners
pages.text: Alex bounded down the stairs. I was less excited. I could hear all the whirring and clanging, the clicking and banging. He seemed used to it, comfortable around it, but I had never heard so many strange noises in my life. It was like he had turned his kitchen into a racing car track. “First,” he announced, “the living room!” Alex’s Dad’s record player had started turning, the needle lowered itself onto the vinyl to play some music. Around us, the lamps and armchairs started to wobble! When I looked closely, I could see bolts attached to the chair legs that pushed up and down, timed to the record that was playing. Alex extended his arm out to present them to me. “These are my dance partners,” he said. I liked the song, but it was hard to hear it against all the noises around us. The slamming of the furniture was making the music jump and, as impressed as I was, I wasn’t convinced that those lamps and chairs were dancing. If anything, it felt like they were marching toward us…
pages.imageAlt: A pixel-art living room with a record player, armchairs and lamps.

pages.heading: The Kitchen
pages.text: Next, he showed me the kitchen. A handle was attached to the toaster. It had pulled the lever down, starting the timer. “That’s my live-in chef,” Alex joked. “and this,” he continued, “is my table tennis buddy.” He walked over to an electronic catapult that was strapped to the kitchen island. It was already pulled back but there was nothing attached for it to throw. Then, Alex picked up a bucket of soft little tennis balls from the floor and perched them just under the catapult. “Grab a paddle,” he said. There was one at my end of the island. I was feeling a lot like I was back on holiday with my cousins.
pages.imageAlt: A pixel-art catapult on a kitchen worktop, loaded with a tennis ball.

pages.heading: Table Tennis
pages.text: The catapult circled through the bucket of tennis balls and flung one forward in my direction! I batted it away. The ball bounced back into the bucket before the catapult grabbed another and sent it my way! “OK,” I admitted. “this is quite fun. But how did you do all of this?” “Well…” Alex’s excitement faded away for a second. He looked distant and wandered away from the catapult to fiddle with some of the kitchen drawers while he spoke. “I … had a lot of time.” My attention had been drawn away from the tennis ball catapult, and I was struggling to keep up with the flying balls. Suddenly, one of them hit my forehead!

pages.heading: Out of Control
pages.text: Alex’s head darted up. “What was that?” “Can you put this back on the slow setting, Alex?” “There is only one setting,” Alex said in a serious tone. I tried to look at him but was struggling to keep up with the game. The catapult was getting faster! Alex tried to get closer to the end of the island so he could grab the bucket but it was too late. The catapult was going crazy, sending tennis balls flying in every direction! “Duck!” I shouted. A plate shattered. “We need to go upstairs and turn it off!” Alex yelled. BANG! BANG! BANG! The cupboard doors were being pelted. The toaster was sizzling… “The chef!” yelled Alex. It was keeping a firm hold on the lever. The toast was burning, and dark smoke clouded the room. Then, of course, the smoke alarm went off. I wafted smoke out of my face and tried to dodge tennis balls, while Alex tried to force his “live-in chef” away from the toaster. “This is bad,” he whined.
pages.imageAlt: A pixel-art boy with a table tennis bat being pelted with tennis balls in a kitchen.

pages.heading: The Furniture
pages.text: I grabbed his arm and dragged him away from the toaster, covering my mouth. “Let’s just get upstairs and shut this thing down,” I said. It was then that I started to hear all those noises again. That banging and slamming. The furniture… The lamps had made their way out of the living room. Some of them were broken and their wires were straining, causing crackles of electricity. The armchair had become stuck in the doorway and was smacking back and forth against it aggressively. I tripped over a smaller lamp and nearly got some sparks of electricity in my face. Alex got his foot caught under a wire and fell over. Some of the dancing furniture was already unplugged but it still was not stopping! I grabbed some of the stray leads and used them to pull the lamps to the ground. The smoke was making its way into the hallway. Alex was halfway up the stairs and I had just made it to the second step. “Come on!” yelled Alex.
pages.imageAlt: A pixel-art living room in chaos, with tangled wires and knocked-over furniture.

pages.heading: Shut Down
pages.text: By the time I reached his room, he was already typing away at his computer, which had finally begun to smoke and steam. We were coughing and wheezing and Alex’s typing wasn’t helping. “I made it do too much at once! It’s over-heated - it won’t shut down!” he said, panicking. “There has to be something we can do!” I shouted. Alex was already under his desk, pulling a seemingly infinite number of leads and wires out of their sockets. Eventually, he pulled the right one. The computer screen flashed to black, then hissed to sleep. The humming from the walls faded to silence and the floor’s vibrations sputtered to a stop. The chaos was over.
pages.imageAlt: A pixel-art old computer on fire and smoking on a messy desk.

pages.heading: Friends
pages.text: Alex sat defeated under his desk. “I just wanted some friends this summer,” he confessed in a hushed tone. “Well… you have some,” I said, “I’ve been texting you all break.” “But you weren’t here,” he replied. “I’m here now and none of us are ever that far away.” I’m not sure he believed me but I didn’t know what else to say. We tidied the house and I stayed until his parents got home. We explained everything together and they were actually pretty understanding. They spoke to Alex after I left. He never told me what they said, or if they were mad, but he seemed much happier the next time I saw him. As for the rest of summer, we went out a few times. We saw a film, went to the park, popped round to each other’s houses. It wasn’t the best summer ever, but it was nice, ordinary, perfectly normal. Of course, after Alex’s home went crazy, that was all either of us wanted!
pages.imageAlt: A pixel-art picture of two friends laughing together at the cinema.

glossary.competitive: Always wanting to win or be the best.
glossary.recoiled: Pulled back suddenly, in fear or dislike.
glossary.whirring: A steady buzzing sound, like a machine turning.
glossary.modified: Changed to work in a different way.
glossary.retro: Old-fashioned, in the style of years ago.
glossary.catapult: A machine that throws things through the air.
glossary.infinite: Without end; too many to count.
